title: Intelligence
summary: What intelligence is, one general ability versus many, Sternberg's problem-solving steps, fluid and crystallised and tacit intelligence, IQ calculation, and heredity versus environment.

lesson.title: Defining intelligence
lesson.hook: Your classmate scores 320 in JAMB but cannot fix a puncture. The vulcaniser at the junction left school early but can diagnose any tyre in seconds. Which of them is intelligent?

slides.heading: What intelligence means
slides.body:
**Intelligence** is a person's cognitive ability to **learn from experience**, **reason well** and **cope with the demands of daily life**. It concerns how well someone deals with the world around them.

Psychologists agree on this broad idea but disagree sharply on a deeper question: is intelligence **one general ability** or **many separate ones**?

slides.heading: Galton and the general factor
slides.body:
**Sir Francis Galton** popularised the study of intelligence in the late 1800s and believed it was largely **inherited**.

The idea of a single **general factor (g)** underlying all specific abilities is most associated with **Charles Spearman** (1904). If you have high g, you are more likely to do well at mechanical, musical, artistic and other tasks. (Your course notes credit this view to Galton.)

left.title: Single general factor
points: Bright people tend to be bright at most things

right.title: Many separate abilities
points: Most people are stronger in some than others

slides.heading: Thurstone and Guilford
slides.body:
**Louis Thurstone (1938)** offered an alternative to general tests: the **Primary Mental Abilities** test, measuring **seven** separate intellectual abilities, such as verbal comprehension, numerical ability and spatial ability.

**J. P. Guilford** went further, proposing that some **150** distinct abilities make up intelligence.

slides.question: Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities test measured how many abilities?
slides.why: Thurstone measured seven primary abilities; Guilford proposed about 150.

terms.meaning: Words and language; numbers and logic
Sensitivity to rhythm, pitch and melody
Visualising and manipulating space and images
Understanding others; understanding and managing oneself

slides.heading: Why Gardner matters
slides.body:
**Howard Gardner (1983)** argued these intelligences are **independent** and handled by **different parts of the brain**. His view is far **broader** than traditional ones: great musical skill or emotional self-understanding counts as intelligence just as much as maths.

Most IQ tests measure only **verbal** and **logical-mathematical** ability, so they miss much of what Gardner includes.

slides.question: According to Gardner, most traditional IQ tests measure mainly:
slides.why: Standard tests focus on verbal and logical-maths skills, missing the other intelligences Gardner describes.

slides.heading: Three gifted classmates
slides.story: In one SS3 class, Adaeze tops every maths test, Bolaji composes songs that the whole school sings, and Musa is the student everyone goes to when they are upset because he always knows what to say. A traditional IQ test would rate Adaeze highest. Gardner would say all three are intelligent, in different ways.
slides.takeaway: Gardner's theory recognises musical and interpersonal strengths that traditional tests ignore.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'explain the different types of intelligence' (list Gardner's seven) and objectives on who said what: Thurstone seven primary abilities, Guilford about 150, Gardner seven intelligences. Trap: confusing Thurstone's seven with Gardner's seven. Thurstone's were test-measured mental abilities; Gardner's include music, body and social skills.
slides.sampleQuestion: Which of the following is NOT one of Gardner's original seven intelligences? (a) musical (b) interpersonal (c) bodily-kinaesthetic (d) mechanical-reflexive
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (d). List all seven in essays and note that standard IQ tests cover only two of them.

points: Intelligence: learning from experience, reasoning well, coping with life.
General factor view: one ability (g) underlies others (Spearman; Galton stressed heredity).
Gardner (1983): seven independent intelligences in different brain areas.
IQ tests mainly measure verbal and logical-mathematical ability.

questions.stem: Intelligence is best defined as the ability to:
options: Learn from experience, reason well and cope with daily demands
questions.explanation: This is the standard broad definition used in the course.

questions.stem: Who proposed seven independent types of intelligence in 1983?
questions.explanation: Howard Gardner proposed multiple intelligences in 1983.

questions.stem: Galton believed intelligence was mainly:
questions.explanation: Galton emphasised heredity.

questions.stem: Guilford suggested that intelligence is made up of about:
questions.explanation: Guilford proposed around 150 distinct abilities.

questions.stem: The view that one general factor underlies specific abilities predicts that a person with high general intelligence will:
options: Tend to do well across many types of task
questions.explanation: A strong general factor supports many specific abilities.

questions.stem: Most traditional IQ tests focus on which of Gardner's intelligences?
questions.explanation: Standard tests concentrate on language and logic-maths skills.

questions.stem: A footballer with exceptional body control but average maths would be rated highly in Gardner's:
questions.explanation: Skilled body movement is bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence.

questions.stem: A counsellor who reads people's feelings accurately and helps them work through conflict shows strong:
questions.explanation: Understanding and relating to others is interpersonal intelligence.

questions.stem: A student who understands her own moods and manages them well shows:
questions.explanation: Self-understanding and adjustment is intrapersonal intelligence.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Thurstone developed the Primary Mental Abilities test of seven abilities.

questions.stem: Gardner claimed his different intelligences are:
options: Mediated by different parts of the brain
questions.explanation: He linked each intelligence to distinct brain systems.

questions.stem: All of the following are among Gardner's seven intelligences EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Mechanical is not one of Gardner's seven.

questions.stem: I. Gardner's view of intelligence is broader than the traditional view. II. Thurstone supported a single general factor. III. Most people are stronger in some abilities than others, say multiple-ability theorists. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Thurstone offered an alternative to general-factor tests.

questions.stem: A critic argues Gardner's 'musical intelligence' is really a talent, not intelligence. This criticism questions:
options: How broadly intelligence should be defined
questions.explanation: The debate is about whether such skills belong under 'intelligence' at all.

questions.stem: Which finding would most support a strong general factor of intelligence?
options: Each ability is completely unrelated to others
People's scores on very different tests are positively correlated
IQ tests measure only verbal skills
questions.explanation: If people who do well on one test tend to do well on others, a shared general factor is likely.

sections.name: Problem-solving steps and kinds of intelligence

lesson.title: How intelligent people solve problems
lesson.hook: Two students face the same tricky analogy question. One rushes and gets it wrong; the other spends longer reading it, then races through the rest. Who is the better reasoner?

slides.heading: Sternberg's componential view
slides.body:
**Robert Sternberg (1979)** proposed that intelligence can be understood through the **cognitive steps** we use in **reasoning and problem-solving**: the **components** of intelligence.

Breaking problem-solving into steps lets researchers find which components make one person a better reasoner than another.

steps.title: Encode
steps.detail: Take in all the relevant information about the problem and store it in usable form.

steps.title: Infer
steps.detail: Work out the relationship between the terms of the problem.

steps.title: Map
steps.detail: Identify common features between relevant pairs of elements.

steps.title: Apply
steps.detail: Use the relationship you identified on the new case.

slides.heading: Good reasoners encode slowly
slides.body:
A surprising finding: **better reasoners spend more time encoding** the problem than poor reasoners, but are **faster at every other step**.

Careful understanding at the start pays off: once the problem is clearly grasped, inferring, mapping and applying go quickly and accurately.

slides.question: According to Sternberg, better reasoners compared with poor reasoners:
options: Spend more time encoding but are faster at other steps
slides.why: Good reasoners invest time in encoding, then move faster through the remaining components.

slides.heading: The analogy question
slides.story: 'Lagos is to Nigeria as Accra is to ____?' Chidi reads carefully (encode), sees Lagos is Nigeria's biggest city (infer), checks Accra is Ghana's biggest city (map), applies the rule (apply), rules out 'Kumasi' and 'Togo' (compare), and writes 'Ghana' (respond). He took longer to read, then answered quickly.
slides.takeaway: Sternberg's components describe the steps of reasoning, and careful encoding speeds up the rest.

right.title: Crystallised
points: Stays stable or grows with age

slides.heading: Intelligence across the lifespan
slides.body:
The fluid-crystallised distinction, developed by Raymond **Cattell** and John **Horn**, shows how intellect changes with **age**. **Fluid** ability, learning new skills for new problems, tends to **decline from middle age**.

**Crystallised** ability, built on knowledge and experience, holds steady or even **increases**. That is why an elderly judge may outperform a young lawyer on legal reasoning but struggle with a new phone app.

slides.question: Solving a brand-new kind of puzzle you have never seen before mainly uses:
slides.why: Fluid intelligence handles novel problems; crystallised intelligence applies learned skills.

slides.heading: Tacit (everyday) intelligence
slides.body:
IQ tests like the Stanford-Binet and Wechsler mainly predict **school performance** and success in **complex occupations**. They say little about skills not taught in school: **fishing, photography, vulcanising** and many trades.

**Sternberg and Wagner (1993)** called this **tacit** or **everyday intelligence**: practical, often informally learned know-how. Tests of tacit intelligence are **specific to a domain** and predict who will do well **in that domain**.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'explain the cognitive steps in reasoning' (all six, in order) and 'explain tacit intelligence'. Objectives test fluid versus crystallised with age scenarios. Trap: thinking better reasoners are faster at encoding; they are slower there and faster elsewhere.
slides.sampleQuestion: Which of the following correctly orders Sternberg's steps? (a) infer, encode, apply, map, compare, respond (b) encode, infer, map, apply, compare, respond (c) encode, map, infer, compare, apply, respond (d) respond, compare, apply, map, infer, encode
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Define each step briefly and add the finding about encoding time.

points: Sternberg: encode, infer, map, apply, compare, respond.
Better reasoners spend longer encoding, then go faster.
Fluid: new problems, declines from middle age; crystallised: learned skills, holds up.
IQ tests predict school and complex jobs, not trade skills.

questions.stem: The first step in Sternberg's problem-solving components is:
questions.explanation: Encoding the relevant information comes first.

questions.stem: The ability to use previously learned skills to solve familiar problems is:
questions.explanation: Crystallised intelligence draws on accumulated knowledge.

questions.stem: Practical, everyday know-how specific to a domain is called:
questions.explanation: Tacit intelligence is practical, domain-specific knowledge.

questions.stem: Fluid intelligence tends to:
questions.explanation: The ability to tackle new problems declines from middle age.

questions.stem: In Sternberg's model, 'map' refers to:
options: Identifying common features between relevant pairs of elements
questions.explanation: Mapping finds shared characteristics between pairs.

questions.stem: General IQ tests like the Stanford-Binet mainly predict:
questions.explanation: They predict school and complex job performance, not trade skills.

questions.stem: A retired professor easily answers questions on history but struggles to learn a new video game. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Crystallised knowledge holds with age while fluid ability for novel tasks declines.

questions.stem: A vulcaniser who left school early diagnoses tyre faults faster than any engineer. This best shows:
questions.explanation: Practical, domain-specific skill not taught in school is tacit intelligence.

questions.stem: A student reads an exam question twice, slowly, then answers quickly and correctly. According to Sternberg, she is likely a:
options: Good reasoner who invests time in encoding
questions.explanation: Good reasoners spend more time encoding and less on later steps.

questions.stem: Which ordering of Sternberg's components is correct?
options: Encode, map, infer, apply, respond, compare
Infer, encode, map, compare, apply, respond
Encode, infer, map, apply, compare, respond
Map, encode, infer, apply, compare, respond
questions.explanation: The sequence runs encode, infer, map, apply, compare, respond.

questions.stem: Sternberg and Wagner (1993) argued that tests of tacit intelligence are useful because they:
options: Predict who will perform well in a specific domain
questions.explanation: Domain-specific tests predict performance in that field.

questions.stem: All of the following are Sternberg's problem-solving components EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: 'Memorise' is not one of the six components.

questions.stem: I. Better reasoners are faster at encoding. II. Crystallised intelligence relies on past learning. III. Fluid intelligence handles novel problems. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: II and III are correct. Better reasoners are slower, not faster, at encoding.

questions.stem: Why might a company hiring photographers prefer a test of tacit intelligence to a general IQ test?
options: Tacit tests predict performance in that specific domain better
questions.explanation: General IQ tests poorly predict skill in areas not taught in school.

questions.stem: Why does Sternberg's component approach help explain individual differences in intelligence?
options: It shows which specific steps make one person a better reasoner than another
It is based on heredity alone
questions.explanation: Breaking reasoning into steps reveals where people differ.

lesson.title: Numbers, genes and upbringing
lesson.hook: A 10-year-old answers questions as well as the average 12-year-old. What is her IQ, and how much of it came from her parents' genes versus the books in her home?

slides.heading: The first useful test
slides.body:
**Alfred Binet**, working with Théodore Simon, produced the first useful intelligence test in **1905** to identify French schoolchildren needing extra help. (Your course notes give 1903.)

**Lewis Terman** of **Stanford University** revised it in 1916 as the **Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale**. **David Wechsler** later created the **Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC)** and the **Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS)**.

slides.heading: Mental age
slides.body:
Binet scored a test by counting correct answers and asking: at what **age** is this the **average** score? That age is the child's **mental age (MA)**.

If a child answers 18 items, and 18 is the average for children aged 8 years 6 months, their MA is 8 years 6 months. MA **above** actual (chronological) age suggests a **bright** child; MA **below** suggests **below-average** ability.

slides.heading: The IQ formula
slides.body:
To compare children of different ages, divide **mental age (MA)** by **chronological age (CA)** and multiply by **100** to remove decimals:

**IQ = MA ÷ CA × 100**

If MA equals CA, IQ is **100**: exactly average. Above 100 is above average; below 100 is below average.

steps.title: Watch the order
steps.detail: Always mental age on top, chronological age underneath.

slides.question: A child has a mental age of 9 and a chronological age of 12. The IQ is:
slides.why: 9 ÷ 12 × 100 = 75. Putting CA on top (12 ÷ 9) would wrongly give 133.

slides.heading: Heredity: twin studies
slides.body:
Research shows **heredity and experience combine** to shape intelligence. **Identical (monozygotic)** twins, who share all their genes, have IQ scores **far more similar** than **fraternal (dizygotic)** twins, even when both pairs grow up in the same intellectual environment.

Since the environments are similar, the extra similarity of identical twins points to **genes**.

right.title: Adoption studies
points: Less like adoptive parents who raised them

slides.heading: Environment matters too
slides.body:
Genes are not the whole story. Children's **interaction with caregivers**, exposure to the adult world of talk, books and problem-solving, is essential for intellectual development.

Intelligence can be **boosted** by **enriching** young children's environments: reading together, conversation, play and good schooling. IQ scores around the world have also risen over generations, too fast for genes alone to explain.

slides.question: Adopted children's IQs tend to resemble those of:
options: Their adoptive parents more than their biological parents
Their biological parents more than their adoptive parents
slides.why: Greater resemblance to biological parents they never lived with points to a genetic influence.

slides.heading: Separated sisters
slides.story: Twin sisters are separated at birth: one raised in Enugu by a teacher's family full of books, the other in a village with little schooling. As adults, both are quick thinkers with similar test patterns, yet the first scores noticeably higher and reads widely. Their shared genes set a similar potential; their environments shaped how far each went.
slides.takeaway: Heredity and environment work together: genes shape potential, and enrichment helps realise it.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: IQ calculation is almost guaranteed: practise MA ÷ CA × 100 and interpret the result. Also expect 'contributing factors to intelligence': heredity (twin and adoption studies) and environment (caregiver interaction, enrichment). Trap: reversing MA and CA in the formula.
slides.sampleQuestion: What is the intelligence quotient of a child whose MA is 14 and CA is 12? Interpret the result.
slides.howToAnswer: 14 ÷ 12 × 100 ≈ 116.7, which is above average. Mention that IQ above 100 means mental age exceeds chronological age.

points: Binet's test led to the Stanford-Binet (Terman) and Wechsler scales.
Mental age: the age for which a score is average.
Twin and adoption studies show a strong genetic influence.
Caregiver interaction and enrichment also raise intelligence.

questions.stem: The formula for the ratio IQ is:
questions.explanation: Mental age divided by chronological age, times 100.

questions.stem: The Stanford-Binet scale was developed by revising Binet's test. Who revised it?
questions.explanation: Terman at Stanford University revised Binet's test.

questions.stem: An IQ of 100 means a person's mental age is:
questions.explanation: MA equal to CA gives an IQ of 100, exactly average.

questions.stem: A child with MA 10 and CA 8 has an IQ of:
The Wechsler scale designed for children is the:
questions.explanation: WISC is the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children; WAIS is for adults.

questions.stem: Identical twins' IQ scores are more similar than fraternal twins' scores. This mainly suggests a role for:
questions.explanation: Identical twins share all their genes, so greater similarity points to heredity.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old answers as well as the average 15-year-old. The IQ is:
A 10-year-old's mental age is 7. The IQ and its interpretation are:
questions.explanation: 7 ÷ 10 × 100 = 70, below average.

questions.stem: Adopted children's IQs resemble their biological parents' more than their adoptive parents'. This supports:
questions.explanation: Resemblance to parents they never lived with points to genetic influence.

questions.stem: Which statement about heredity and intelligence is MOST accurate?
options: Intelligence is fully fixed by genes
Heredity and experience combine to determine intelligence
questions.explanation: Both genes and environment contribute.

questions.stem: All of the following can help enhance children's intelligence EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Isolation deprives children of the interaction that supports intellectual growth.

questions.stem: Why did Binet's mental age need to be converted into an IQ?
options: To compare children of different chronological ages
To remove the need for testing
questions.explanation: Dividing by chronological age allows comparison across ages.

questions.stem: A child with MA 14 and CA 12 has an IQ of about:
questions.explanation: 14 ÷ 12 × 100 ≈ 116.7, above average.

questions.stem: I. Identical twins raised together have more similar IQs than fraternal twins raised together. II. Enrichment cannot change intelligence. III. Adoption studies point to heredity. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Enrichment can enhance intelligence.

questions.stem: Why do psychologists compare identical and fraternal twins raised in the same home?
options: Because identical twins have different genes
Because fraternal twins share all genes
Because their environments are similar, so extra similarity in identical twins can be linked to genes
questions.explanation: Holding environment roughly constant lets researchers attribute the extra similarity to shared genes.
